issues.subcategory: Contradictory sample source and sampling design
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the study as using a national probability or nationally representative general-population sample, but the Methods state that participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool and were mostly 19-year-old students. These are mutually incompatible sampling frames. This affects every claim about representativeness, generalizability, sample size, weighting, attrition, and replication.
issues.quote: Abstract: "We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years." Methods: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington." Discussion: "We assessed how SDO, RWA, and environmentalism are related over time in a general population sample."

issues.subcategory: Unsupported national representativeness claims
issues.description: The actual described sample is young, mostly female, and predominantly Pākehā, which is not representative of the New Zealand population. Claims that the findings are highly generalisable to New Zealand are therefore unsupported unless the authors clarify that this is actually a probability sample, provide sampling weights, and resolve the contradiction with the student-pool description.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European)."; "Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population."

issues.subcategory: Time frame inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between describing the study as spanning five years and as using data from five semesters. Five semesters is not equivalent to five years, and the spacing between waves is central to interpreting cross-lagged effects. The manuscript does not clearly report whether the waves were annual, semesterly, or irregular.
issues.quote: "The influence of social dominance orientation and right-wing authoritarianism on environmentalism: A five-year cross-lagged analysis"; "This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."

issues.subcategory: Impossible confidence intervals and p-values for stated N
issues.description: The Time 1 correlations and confidence intervals are incompatible with the stated sample size of N = 374. For example, r = .21 with N = 374 would have an approximate 95% CI around [.11, .30], not [.18, .23]. Likewise, r = -.08 with N = 374 would not be p < .001. The mean confidence intervals are also far too narrow for N = 374. This suggests either the wrong sample size is reported, the table is based on another dataset, or the confidence intervals/p-values are miscomputed.

issues.subcategory: Model fit statistics inconsistent with stated N and chi-square
issues.description: The reported RMSEA is mathematically inconsistent with the reported chi-square, degrees of freedom, and N = 374. Using χ² = 36511.73, df = 2279, and N = 374 gives an RMSEA near .20, not .03. The reported RMSEA would imply an enormous sample size, again suggesting that the reported N, model fit, or both are incorrect.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study..."; "χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07)"

issues.subcategory: Degrees of freedom inconsistent with described model
issues.description: The Methods describe a path analysis with three variables measured at five time points, which would involve 15 observed variables if scale scores were used. A model with only 15 observed variables cannot have 2,279 degrees of freedom. The df implies an item-level latent variable model, but the manuscript does not describe such a measurement model. This prevents readers from understanding or evaluating the analysis.
issues.quote: "The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus"; "χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001"

issues.subcategory: Poor model fit accepted without adequate justification
issues.description: The CFI of .86 is conventionally poor or at least below common thresholds for acceptable fit. The authors dismiss this because CFI is said to be affected by model complexity and accept the model based on RMSEA/SRMR, but the RMSEA itself appears inconsistent with the reported N and χ². Poor fit undermines interpretation of all cross-lagged coefficients.
issues.quote: "Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted."

issues.subcategory: Environmentalism measure does not match stated construct
issues.description: The manuscript says the outcome is willingness to change behavior or willingness to sacrifice for the environment, but the Measures section says environmentalism was measured using concern about the environment and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. Concern and skepticism/exaggeration are not the same construct as willingness to sacrifice or behavioral change. This is a central construct validity problem because the conclusions are framed around willingness to act, sacrifice, and exploit the environment.
issues.quote: Abstract: "people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment"; Measures: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'"; Data Analysis: "willingness to sacrifice for the environment"

issues.subcategory: Broad climate-change claims from generic environmental items
issues.description: The Introduction and Discussion repeatedly frame the study around climate change denial and climate mitigation, but the outcome items refer to the current state of the natural environment and whether environmental problems have been exaggerated. These items are not specific to climate change, climate policy, or climate mitigation behavior. The manuscript therefore overextends the operationalization to climate change-specific conclusions.
issues.quote: "Research on the psychological foundations of climate change denial have highlighted the important role of two ideological attitudes"; "While climate change is arguably the biggest environmental problem of our time..."; "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?"; "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?"

issues.subcategory: Environmental exploitation not measured
issues.description: The abstract and discussion infer a motivation to exploit the environment, but the study measures self-reported concern/exaggeration or willingness to sacrifice, not environmental exploitation, exploitative behavior, or motives. This creates a mismatch between the measured variables and the mechanistic interpretation.
issues.quote: "These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance"; "The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority."

issues.subcategory: Willingness is treated as behavior
issues.description: The manuscript discusses willingness to change behavior as though it directly indexes pro-environmental action, but all measures are self-reported attitudes or intentions. Willingness does not establish actual behavior, behavioral change, or sacrifice.
issues.quote: "people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment"; "The preference for an unequal society leads individuals to be less willing to make personal sacrifices for the environment."

issues.subcategory: Insufficient procedure and sampling details
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide enough procedural information to evaluate or replicate the study: recruitment procedures, inclusion/exclusion criteria, compensation, consent/ethics, survey mode, timing between waves, initial invited sample, response rates, and retention are not reported. Referring readers to a website is not an adequate substitute for reporting core methodological details in the manuscript.
issues.quote: "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.subcategory: Unreported attrition across five waves
issues.description: A five-wave longitudinal study requires detailed reporting of the number of participants invited and retained at each wave, dropout patterns, and whether attrition was associated with SDO, RWA, environmentalism, or demographics. None is provided. Attrition can bias cross-lagged estimates, especially when listwise deletion is used.
issues.quote: "This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."; "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."

issues.subcategory: Listwise deletion without missing-data justification
issues.description: Listwise deletion assumes data are missing completely at random or at least that complete-case analysis is unbiased. The manuscript provides no missingness diagnostics, no comparison of completers versus dropouts, and no rationale for not using full-information maximum likelihood or multiple imputation, which are standard in longitudinal SEM.
issues.quote: "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."

issues.subcategory: Potentially underpowered model for stated N
issues.description: If the sample size is truly N = 374, it is small for a complex five-wave item-level SEM with 2,279 df and many longitudinal constraints. Small samples can produce unstable estimates, convergence problems, and unreliable fit indices, particularly for small cross-lagged effects. No power analysis or precision justification is provided.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study..."; "χ2(2279) = 36511.73"

issues.subcategory: No sample-size or power justification
issues.description: The study tests very small longitudinal cross-lagged effects, but the manuscript provides no a priori or sensitivity power analysis and no rationale for the analytic sample size. This is especially problematic given the inconsistency between the reported N and the extremely precise confidence intervals.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study..."; "Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05"

issues.subcategory: RWA measurement non-equivalence across waves
issues.description: One RWA item was omitted at Time 2 but included at all other waves. This changes the measurement content of RWA across time and threatens longitudinal comparability unless handled with an explicit longitudinal measurement model and invariance testing. The manuscript does not explain how the missing item was modeled or whether Time 2 RWA is comparable to other waves.
issues.quote: "The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points."

issues.subcategory: No longitudinal measurement invariance testing
issues.description: The study draws conclusions about changes and cross-time effects, but there is no report of configural, metric, scalar, or residual invariance for SDO, RWA, or environmentalism across the five waves. Without measurement invariance, observed longitudinal paths may reflect changes in item functioning or scale meaning rather than changes in constructs.
issues.quote: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points"; "we constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time"

issues.subcategory: Incomplete reliability reporting
issues.description: Reliability is reported only for Time 1 in Table 1. Longitudinal analyses require reliability information at every wave, especially because the RWA item set differs at Time 2. Without wave-specific reliabilities, readers cannot assess measurement quality or attenuation across time.
issues.quote: "Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1. Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used"

issues.subcategory: Scale scoring and reverse-coding not described
issues.description: The SDO and environmentalism measures include items in opposite directions, but the manuscript does not explicitly state which items were reverse-coded, how scale scores were formed, how missing items were handled, or whether higher scores consistently represent higher SDO/RWA/environmentalism. This impedes replication and interpretation.
issues.quote: "Three items favoured dominance... and three favoured equality"; "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?"

issues.subcategory: Shortened scales without item-selection rationale
issues.description: The authors use six items from longer SDO and RWA scales but do not explain how the items were selected, whether they preserve the dimensional structure of the full scales, or whether they have been validated for this longitudinal context. This matters because short scales may underrepresent facets of SDO and RWA.
issues.quote: "Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] SDO6 scale."; "Right-wing authoritarianism was assessed with six items from Altemeyer’s [27] RWA scale."

issues.subcategory: RWA subdimensions ignored despite differential predictions
issues.description: The Introduction acknowledges evidence that RWA subdimensions have different and even opposite associations with pro-environmental attitudes, yet the study models RWA as a single aggregate and then interprets it as submission to authority/tradition. This may obscure theoretically important effects and makes the mechanistic interpretation of RWA unsupported.
issues.quote: "Reese [20] found that the dimensions of RWA differentially predict pro-environmental attitudes: authoritarian submission predicts greater pro-environmentalism, authoritarian aggression predicts lower pro-environmentalism, whilst the preference for tradition is unrelated."; "to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority."

issues.subcategory: Stationarity constraints imposed without reported tests
issues.description: The authors constrain cross-lagged paths and residual variances to be time-invariant because of substantive interest, but they do not report whether stationarity is empirically tenable relative to less constrained models. If the effects vary across waves, imposing equality can bias estimates and obscure theoretically important developmental or historical changes.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant."; "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured."

issues.subcategory: Duplicated and unclear constraint description
issues.description: The Methods twice state that the cross-lagged associations were constrained to equality, while also mentioning residual variance constraints. This duplication makes it unclear exactly what model was fitted and which parameters were constrained.
issues.quote: "We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point."

issues.subcategory: No report of correlated item residuals or method effects
issues.description: For repeated use of the same items across waves, longitudinal SEMs commonly allow item-specific residual covariances across time to account for stable item wording/method effects. The manuscript mentions equality constraints on residual variances but does not report correlated residuals. Omitting them can inflate stability estimates, worsen fit, and bias cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: "We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points."

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from observational cross-lagged data
issues.description: The study is observational and based on self-report survey data. Cross-lagged associations do not establish causality because they can be produced by unmeasured stable traits, time-varying confounders, common-method variance, or between-person differences. The manuscript nevertheless repeatedly uses causal language such as 'causal pathway,' 'causal effect,' and 'leads.'
issues.quote: "These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism."; "this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes"; "The preference for an unequal society leads individuals to be less willing to make personal sacrifices for the environment."

issues.subcategory: Uncontrolled confounding
issues.description: The model appears to include only SDO, RWA, and environmentalism. Potential confounders such as political ideology/party support, socioeconomic status, education, gender, ethnicity, age, religiosity, urban/rural residence, and exposure to environmental events are not included. These could plausibly influence both ideological attitudes and environmentalism, biasing cross-lagged estimates.
issues.quote: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points"

issues.subcategory: Authors acknowledge third-variable explanation but retain causal interpretation
issues.description: The Discussion acknowledges that bidirectional associations may be explained by a third variable, but the manuscript still presents causal conclusions elsewhere. This internal tension weakens the interpretation and requires more cautious wording or additional analyses.
issues.quote: "Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable."; "This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future"

issues.subcategory: Traditional CLPM conflates within-person and between-person effects
issues.description: The cross-lagged panel model used here does not separate stable between-person differences from within-person change. Therefore, paths interpreted as changes in an individual’s environmentalism may partly reflect stable between-person associations. A random-intercept CLPM or other within-person longitudinal model would be needed to support claims about intraindividual change.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model"; "These results indicate a bidirectional association between ideology and environmentalism over time"; "SDO and RWA predict change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment"

issues.subcategory: Claim of stronger SDO effect contradicted by nonsignificant model comparison
issues.description: The authors tested whether SDO and RWA differed in predictive ability by constraining the two paths to equality. The reported comparison was nonsignificant, meaning the data do not provide evidence that SDO is statistically stronger than RWA. Despite this, the Results, Discussion, Abstract, and Conclusion repeatedly claim that SDO is the stronger predictor.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor"; "SDO was the strongest ideological predictor of environmentalism"; "SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA."

issues.subcategory: Incorrect statement that Wald test is not possible
issues.description: The manuscript states that a Wald test comparing SDO and RWA paths is not possible because of model constraints. In SEM software such as Mplus, equality constraints and MODEL CONSTRAINT/Wald tests can be used to compare parameters, including under stationarity. If there was a technical reason this specific comparison was impossible, it needs to be explained. As written, the rationale is questionable.
issues.quote: "Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible."

issues.subcategory: Standardized versus unstandardized estimates contradictory
issues.description: The Methods say standardized parameters are presented, while the Figure caption and Results refer to unstandardized parameters and use B coefficients. Standardized and unstandardized estimates answer different questions, especially when comparing effect magnitudes across constructs. This ambiguity affects interpretation of claims that one effect is stronger than another.
issues.quote: "We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances."; "Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment"; "based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients"

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent significance thresholds
issues.description: The Methods state that p < .05 is the significance threshold, but the Figure caption states that all paths meet p < .01 unless noted. This creates ambiguity about the criterion used for inference.
issues.quote: "we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings."; "All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted."

issues.subcategory: Reported estimates, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values inconsistent
issues.description: Several reported coefficients have p-values or confidence intervals that do not align with the reported 'SD' values, which appear to be standard errors. For example, B = -.02 with SD/SE = .01 would not typically yield p = .001; B = -.01 with SD/SE = .002 would generally yield p < .001, not p = .002. The manuscript also labels uncertainty as SD rather than SE. These inconsistencies raise concerns about calculation, transcription, or reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: "SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01])."; "B = -.01, SD = .002, p = .002, 95% CI [-.01, -.003]"

issues.subcategory: Implausible chi-square difference value
issues.description: The reported chi-square difference for the SDO/RWA cross-lag comparison is 15,389.13, which is implausibly enormous given the tiny coefficient difference reported and the stated N = 374. This may be a misplaced comma/decimal, but as written it indicates a serious statistical reporting error.
issues.quote: "These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)"

issues.subcategory: Malformed chi-square notation
issues.description: Several chi-square tests are reported as '2(1)' rather than χ²(1), making the test statistic unclear. Although likely a formatting error, it affects interpretability and should be corrected, especially because the values are central to the claims.

issues.subcategory: Effect-size comparisons across differently scaled constructs
issues.description: The manuscript compares the strength of reciprocal paths using unstandardized coefficients across different dependent variables. Even if variables use the same response scale, their variances, reliabilities, and latent scaling differ, so unstandardized coefficients are not directly comparable without careful standardization or alternative effect-size metrics.
issues.quote: "the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse (2(1) = 39.97, p < .001)"; "based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor"

issues.subcategory: Informal comparison of dependent correlations
issues.description: The authors infer that the SDO-environmentalism correlation is stronger than the RWA-environmentalism correlation because confidence intervals do not overlap. These correlations are dependent because they share the environmentalism variable and SDO and RWA are correlated. A formal test for comparing dependent correlations, such as Steiger's or Williams's test, is required.
issues.quote: "the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval."

issues.subcategory: Large-sample rationale for p-value threshold is inappropriate and inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript says that because the dataset is large, p < .05 was used as the significance threshold. In large samples, trivial effects can become statistically significant, so emphasis should shift toward effect sizes, uncertainty, and practical significance; if anything, stricter thresholds may be considered. The statement is also inconsistent with the reported N = 374.
issues.quote: "Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings."

issues.subcategory: Incomplete presentation of longitudinal results
issues.description: The Results refer readers to Figure 1 for autoregressive and cross-lagged paths, but the manuscript text does not provide the autoregressive coefficients, within-wave covariances, residual correlations, all wave-specific descriptive statistics, or all model estimates needed to evaluate the model. This limits reproducibility and interpretation.
issues.quote: "As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time"; "Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment"

issues.subcategory: No preregistration or analysis-plan transparency
issues.description: The manuscript does not report preregistration, a prospective analysis plan, or which modeling decisions were confirmatory versus exploratory. Given the many researcher degrees of freedom—sample definition, listwise deletion, item selection, stationarity constraints, model fit criteria, equality tests, and interpretation of nonsignificant comparisons—this raises analytic flexibility concerns.
issues.quote: "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects"; "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."; "A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."

issues.subcategory: Analysis syntax unavailable during review
issues.description: The authors state that Mplus syntax will be available only upon acceptance, meaning reviewers and readers cannot currently verify the model specification, constraints, missing-data handling, estimator, or treatment of the omitted RWA item. For a complex SEM with inconsistencies in reporting, current availability is important.
issues.quote: "A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."

issues.subcategory: Estimator and treatment of ordinal items not reported
issues.description: All items use 7-point Likert-type response scales, but the manuscript does not report the SEM estimator, whether items were treated as continuous or ordinal, whether robust standard errors were used, or how non-normality was handled. These choices can affect fit statistics, standard errors, and parameter estimates.
issues.quote: "Participants rated the extent to which they agreed with each item on 7-point Likert scales"; "The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29])."

issues.subcategory: No survey weights or complex-sampling adjustment
issues.description: If the study truly used a national probability sample, the analysis should report whether design weights, post-stratification weights, clustering, or stratification were used. If it was a student sample, such adjustments are irrelevant. The absence of this information further reflects the unresolved sampling contradiction and affects population inference.
issues.quote: "national probability sample"; "Using a nationally representative sample"; "We used path analysis to examine associations"

issues.subcategory: Unsupported inference about national socialization into authoritarianism
issues.description: The finding that RWA predicts later SDO but not vice versa is interpreted as evidence that New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance. A cross-lagged association among self-reported attitudes does not identify a national socialization process, and no socialization variables or contextual mechanisms were measured.
issues.quote: "Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance."

issues.subcategory: Hierarchy-attenuating environmentalism claim exceeds data
issues.description: The manuscript argues that environmentalism is a hierarchy-attenuating ideology because exploitation benefits dominant groups and harms subordinate groups. The study did not measure perceived hierarchy attenuation, group-based distribution of environmental harms, environmental justice beliefs, or policy framing. This theoretical claim may be plausible but is not directly tested by the reported data.
issues.quote: "Gaining similar opposition from Social Dominants, environmentalism is a hierarchy-attenuating ideology: Exploitation of natural resources favours the dominant group, while the consequences fall to those at the bottom of the hierarchy."

issues.subcategory: Common-method self-report bias not addressed
issues.description: All key variables appear to be self-report Likert measures administered in the same survey context. Shared method variance, response styles, acquiescence, and social desirability could contribute to associations among ideology and environmental attitudes. The manuscript does not discuss or attempt to mitigate these issues.
issues.quote: "Participants rated the extent to which they agreed with each item on 7-point Likert scales"; "Participants responded on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much)"

issues.subcategory: No ethics/IRB statement
issues.description: The manuscript does not report ethical approval, informed consent procedures, or participant protections. This is standard reporting for longitudinal human-subjects research.
issues.quote: "Participants and Procedure"

issues.subcategory: Terminology for the environmental variable changes across sections
issues.description: The manuscript alternates among 'environmentalism,' 'concern about environmental problems,' 'willingness to sacrifice,' 'willingness to change behaviour,' and 'environmental sacrifice.' These are not interchangeable constructs. The inconsistent terminology obscures what was actually measured and what the reported paths mean.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems."; "willingness to sacrifice for the environment"; "willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment"; "environmental sacrifice"

issues.subcategory: Discussion claims significant stronger effect despite results saying no difference
issues.description: The Discussion states that SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA, but the Results section reports a nonsignificant equality-constraint test. This is a direct inconsistency between the statistical test and interpretive conclusion.
issues.quote: Results: "2(1) = 2.34, p = .126"; Discussion: "In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA."
